themes.label: AI product judgment
themes.why: Tests whether you can reason about building with genuinely probabilistic, imperfect AI and still ship something users trust.

themes.label: 0-to-1 building
themes.why: Tests whether you can create structure and momentum from nothing, without an existing team, process, or user base to lean on.

themes.label: Root-cause diagnosis
themes.why: Tests your diagnostic rigor — whether you form and test hypotheses systematically or jump to the first plausible story.

themes.label: Funnel optimization
themes.why: Tests whether you can find and fix the highest-leverage step in a multi-step journey, not just the most visible one.

themes.label: Data-driven decisions
themes.why: Tests whether you actually use data to decide, or use it to justify a decision you'd already made.

themes.label: Stakeholder management
themes.why: Tests whether you can align people with competing incentives without just deferring to the loudest voice.

themes.label: Cross-functional alignment
themes.why: Tests whether you can get eng, design, and business functions rowing in the same direction without formal authority over any of them.

themes.label: Influence without authority
themes.why: Tests how you move people who don't report to you and have no obligation to listen.

themes.label: Conflict & disagreement
themes.why: Tests whether disagreement makes you defensive or curious, and whether you can disagree without damaging the relationship.

themes.label: Saying no
themes.why: Tests whether you can protect the roadmap and the team's focus even when the request comes from someone senior or persistent.

themes.label: Killing a project
themes.why: Tests whether you can recognize sunk cost and pull the plug on your own work before it wastes more of the company's resources.

themes.label: Failure & self-awareness
themes.why: Tests whether you can own a real mistake without spiraling into excuses or reaching for false modesty.

themes.label: Ambiguity
themes.why: Tests whether you can make forward progress and a defensible call when there's no clean data or precedent to lean on.

themes.label: Prioritization
themes.why: Tests your judgment on trade-offs when everything looks urgent and resources are fixed.

themes.label: Customer empathy
themes.why: Tests whether your decisions are actually grounded in a real user's context, not an assumption about them.

themes.label: User research
themes.why: Tests whether you know how to extract a genuine insight from users rather than just confirming what you wanted to hear.

themes.label: Metrics ownership
themes.why: Tests whether you can define, move, and defend a number you're accountable for, not just report it.

themes.label: Experimentation
themes.why: Tests your rigor in testing ideas — hypothesis, design, sample size, and honest reading of ambiguous results.

themes.label: Phased launches
themes.why: Tests your judgment on de-risking a rollout without stalling momentum or hiding behind an endless beta.

themes.label: Compliance & risk
themes.why: Tests whether you can hold the line on legal, regulatory, or policy risk even when it slows the product down.

themes.label: Technical depth
themes.why: Tests whether you can go deep enough with engineering to make a real trade-off call, not just defer entirely.

themes.label: Mentoring
themes.why: Tests whether you actively grow the people around you, not just your own output.

themes.label: Giving & receiving feedback
themes.why: Tests whether you can deliver hard feedback constructively and take it without getting defensive.

themes.label: Ethical calls
themes.why: Tests your judgment when the profitable or expedient choice and the right choice for the user diverge.

themes.label: Leadership
themes.why: Tests whether you can rally and unblock a team without formal management authority over its members.

themes.label: Execution under constraint
themes.why: Tests whether you can still ship something real when time, budget, or people get cut out from under you.

themes.label: Career & motivation
themes.why: Tests whether your reasons for this role and this company are genuine and specific, not generic.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to decide whether an AI feature was actually the right solution, versus something simpler.
variants: Walk me through a call you made on whether to use AI at all for a problem
questions.probes: Whether you reach for AI by default or actually weigh it against a deterministic or rules-based baseline first.
pitfalls: Describing the AI build without ever stating what a simpler, non-AI solution would have achieved
Treating 'we used AI' as the impressive part of the story instead of the judgment behind it
followUps: What would have made you choose the non-AI path instead?
How did you validate the AI approach was actually better before committing engineering time to it?

questions.question: Describe a time an AI or ML-powered feature you owned produced a wrong or embarrassing output in front of users. What did you do?
variants: Tell me about a moment your model or AI feature failed publicly
questions.probes: Whether you designed for the probabilistic failure mode in advance, and how you respond operationally when it surfaces in production.
pitfalls: Blaming the model or the data science team instead of owning the product decisions around confidence, fallback, and UX
No mention of what changed in the guardrails after the incident
followUps: What guardrail or eval would have caught this before it reached users?
How did you decide whether to roll back versus patch forward?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you built a product or feature completely from scratch, with no existing playbook to follow.
variants: Walk me through a 0-to-1 you owned end to end
questions.probes: Whether you can create structure, sequence decisions, and get to a shippable V1 without an established process to lean on.
pitfalls: Spending too long on process and research before shipping anything a real user could react to
Describing the build chronologically with no mention of what you deliberately left out of V1
followUps: How did you decide what NOT to build in version one?
What was your very first signal that you were on the right track?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to convince leadership to invest in a brand-new product line with no existing revenue or user data to point to.
variants: Tell me about pitching something net-new when you had no traction numbers to back it up
questions.probes: Whether you can build a credible case from proxy evidence and market signal rather than hiding behind 'trust me.'
pitfalls: Relying purely on passion or conviction with no evidence at all
Overpromising a timeline or revenue number just to get the green light
followUps: What proxy data did you use instead of real usage data?
What was the smallest bet you asked for, and why that size?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to define success metrics for a product that didn't exist yet.
variants: How have you set goals for something with zero historical baseline?
questions.probes: Whether you can reason from first principles and comparable products rather than picking an arbitrary number to look decisive.
pitfalls: Picking a vanity metric because it was easy to measure, not because it reflected real value
No plan for revisiting the metric once real data started coming in
followUps: How did that metric hold up once you had three months of real data?
What would you have set as the goal instead, in hindsight?

questions.question: Walk me through a time you had to build the first version of a product with a team smaller than the scope really required.
variants: Tell me about doing more with less on a brand-new build
questions.probes: Whether you can scope ruthlessly and make real trade-offs rather than just working longer hours to compensate.
pitfalls: Framing it as a heroics story about personal effort instead of the scoping decisions that made it possible
Not naming what got cut
followUps: What's the first thing you'd add back if you got two more engineers?
What broke first because the team was too small?

questions.question: Tell me about launching a product into a market you didn't fully understand yet.
variants: Describe a time you took a product into unfamiliar territory — a new geography, industry, or user type
questions.probes: How you compensated for the knowledge gap — through research, local partners, or fast iteration — rather than assuming your home-market intuition would transfer.
pitfalls: Assuming domestic user behavior would generalize without checking
No specific example of something you got wrong about the new market and had to correct
followUps: What assumption from your home market turned out to be wrong there?
How long did it take to feel like you actually understood the market?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you diagnosed a sudden, unexplained drop in a key metric.
variants: Walk me through a time the numbers went wrong and you had to find out why
questions.probes: Whether you worked through hypotheses systematically — ruling out data artifacts, segmenting before guessing — rather than jumping to the first plausible story.
pitfalls: Narrating the timeline without naming the hypotheses you ruled out
Jumping straight to 'we shipped X, it must be that' without checking if the drop was even real
followUps: What would have caught it earlier?
What was the one hypothesis you were most confident in that turned out to be wrong?

questions.question: Describe a time a metric looked broken but turned out to be a data or instrumentation issue, not a real problem.
variants: Tell me about a false alarm you had to run down and rule out
questions.probes: Whether you validate data integrity before treating a metric move as a real signal — a common trap even for senior PMs.
pitfalls: Spending days building a fix for a problem that never actually existed
Not describing how you eventually figured out it was a data issue
followUps: What tipped you off that it might be a data issue rather than real?
What did you change in your process after that?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you found and fixed the biggest drop-off point in a user funnel.
variants: Walk me through improving conversion at a specific step in a multi-step flow
questions.probes: Whether you can isolate the real bottleneck with data rather than optimizing the step that's easiest to change or most visible to leadership.
pitfalls: Optimizing the top of the funnel because it's more visible, while a downstream step was the real leak
No quantified before/after impact
followUps: How did you rule out that the drop-off was a symptom of an earlier step, not that step itself?
What was the actual lift, and how did you attribute it to your change specifically?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to choose between optimizing for funnel conversion and optimizing for a different goal, like long-term retention or trust.
variants: Tell me about a trade-off between conversion rate and something else that mattered more
questions.probes: Whether you understand that a locally-optimized funnel can hurt the business — dark patterns, mismatched expectations — and can articulate that trade-off explicitly.
pitfalls: Chasing the conversion number in isolation with no mention of downstream effects (refunds, churn, support load)
Presenting it as a clean win with no acknowledgment of the trade-off
followUps: How did you measure the downstream effect on retention or trust?
Where's the line for you between persuasive design and a dark pattern?

questions.question: Tell me about a decision you made that went against what the data seemed to be telling you.
variants: Walk me through a time you overrode the numbers with judgment
questions.probes: Whether you can articulate a defensible reason — a flaw in the data, a longer time horizon, a qualitative signal — rather than just ignoring evidence you didn't like.
pitfalls: Framing it as 'trusting your gut' with no articulated reasoning for why the data was insufficient
Not mentioning how the decision actually played out afterward
followUps: How did you know you weren't just rationalizing a decision you'd already made?
How did it turn out — were you right?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to make a significant product call with data that was incomplete or actively conflicting.
variants: Tell me about a decision where the numbers you had didn't clearly point one way
questions.probes: How you weigh partial or contradictory evidence and still commit to a call, rather than waiting indefinitely for more data.
pitfalls: Treating incomplete data as an excuse for inaction
No mention of what would have changed your mind
followUps: What was the minimum evidence bar you set for yourself to act?
What additional data, if you'd had it, would have changed the call?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you used data to kill an idea that you personally liked or had championed.
variants: Describe a moment the numbers told you your own idea was wrong
questions.probes: Intellectual honesty — whether you can let go of a personal favorite when the evidence doesn't support it.
pitfalls: Downplaying how attached you actually were to the idea, making the letting-go sound trivial
No specifics on the actual metric or evidence that changed your mind
followUps: How long did it take you to accept the data once you saw it?
What did you do with the resources that were freed up?

questions.question: Walk me through a time you had to present a data-backed recommendation to an audience that was skeptical of the data itself.
variants: Tell me about convincing a room that didn't trust your numbers
questions.probes: Whether you can build credibility for the data — methodology, sample size, source — rather than just repeating the conclusion louder.
pitfalls: Getting defensive about the data instead of addressing the specific skepticism
No mention of what, if anything, was legitimate about their skepticism
followUps: What was the strongest objection they raised, and was it valid?
Did you change your methodology afterward because of that pushback?

questions.question: Tell me about a time a small sample size or noisy result nearly led you to the wrong conclusion.
variants: Describe a time you almost over-read a result that wasn't statistically solid
questions.probes: Statistical judgment — whether you understand significance, sample size, and confidence intervals well enough to catch your own false positive.
pitfalls: Not explaining the actual statistical issue in plain terms
Taking credit for catching it if someone else actually caught it first
followUps: What made you double-check the result instead of just acting on it?
What's your rule of thumb now for how much data is enough?

questions.question: Tell me about your toughest stakeholder and how you tackled them.
variants: Who's been the hardest person to manage as a stakeholder, and how did you get them aligned?
Describe your most difficult stakeholder relationship and how you handled it
questions.probes: Whether you adapted your approach to the specific person's incentives and communication style, rather than just repeating your standard pitch louder.
pitfalls: Blaming the stakeholder's personality instead of showing what you changed in your own approach
No resolution — the story ends at the conflict with no outcome
followUps: What was different about how you communicated with them versus everyone else on the project?
Is the relationship still difficult today, or did it fundamentally change?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to manage a difficult, senior executive who kept pushing their own opinion over your product judgment.
variants: Tell me about handling a VP or C-level exec who disagreed with your product direction
questions.probes: Whether you can hold your ground on product judgment with someone senior to you, using evidence and framing rather than either capitulating or getting into a standoff.
pitfalls: Simply deferring to the executive's opinion and calling that 'stakeholder management'
Describing the exec as simply wrong with no acknowledgment of what valid concern was underneath their pushback
followUps: What did you concede, and what did you hold firm on?
How did the relationship evolve after that disagreement?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to manage stakeholders across multiple time zones or geographies with different priorities.
variants: Describe aligning stakeholders who weren't even working the same hours as you
questions.probes: Whether you built processes (async updates, clear documentation, decision logs) to bridge the gap rather than relying on live meetings alone.
pitfalls: No mention of specific process or tooling used to bridge the time-zone gap
Framing the time-zone difference as purely a burden with no acknowledgment of what it forced you to do better
followUps: What async process did you put in place to keep everyone aligned?
What broke down before you fixed the process?

questions.question: Walk me through a time a key stakeholder lost trust in you or your team, and how you rebuilt it.
variants: Tell me about repairing a stakeholder relationship after it went bad
questions.probes: Whether you can diagnose the actual root of the broken trust and take ownership, rather than just being extra nice going forward.
pitfalls: Vague platitudes about 'communicating more' with no concrete change described
Not naming what originally broke the trust
followUps: What specifically caused the trust to break in the first place?
How do you know the trust is actually rebuilt, not just quieter?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to say no to a stakeholder's request while keeping the relationship intact.
variants: Describe pushing back on a stakeholder without damaging the relationship
questions.probes: Whether you can decline a request with a clear, respectful rationale and an alternative, rather than a flat refusal or a reluctant yes.
pitfalls: Framing the no as purely their loss with no acknowledgment of their underlying need
Caving after minor pushback, undermining the credibility of the original no
followUps: What did you offer them instead of what they originally asked for?
How did they react in the moment, versus a few weeks later?

questions.question: Tell me about a time engineering, design, and business stakeholders were all misaligned on the same project, and how you got them on the same page.
variants: Describe a project where every function wanted something different and you had to reconcile it
questions.probes: Whether you can find the underlying shared goal beneath surface-level disagreement and translate between functions with different incentives.
pitfalls: Just picking one side's opinion and calling it alignment
No mention of the actual mechanism used to reconcile the views — a shared doc, a working session, a reframed goal
followUps: What was the shared goal that got everyone to agree?
How long did the misalignment go undetected before you addressed it?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to work closely with a function you'd never partnered with before — legal, finance, sales ops — to ship something.
variants: Tell me about collaborating with an unfamiliar function to get a product out
questions.probes: Whether you can quickly learn a new function's language and constraints rather than treating them as a rubber-stamp step.
pitfalls: Treating the unfamiliar function as an obstacle to route around instead of a genuine collaborator
No specific detail about what you learned about how that function actually operates
followUps: What did you get wrong initially about how that function worked?
What would you do differently starting that collaboration again?

questions.question: Tell me about a launch that slipped because two functions weren't actually aligned on scope, even though everyone thought they were.
variants: Describe a time 'alignment' turned out to be an illusion and it cost you a deadline
questions.probes: Whether you can spot the difference between agreement in a meeting and true shared understanding, and what you changed in your process afterward.
pitfalls: Blaming the other function for 'not really listening' with no reflection on your own communication gap
No process change described for future projects
followUps: What signal, in hindsight, would have told you the alignment wasn't real?
What do you do differently now to confirm alignment before it's too late?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to get a team to prioritize your work when they had no formal obligation to listen to you.
variants: Describe influencing a team you had zero authority over
questions.probes: Whether you built genuine buy-in — through shared incentives, credibility, or relationship — rather than escalating to someone's manager as the first move.
pitfalls: Jumping straight to escalation instead of trying to build the case directly first
No mention of what was in it for the other team
followUps: What did the other team actually get out of prioritizing your work?
When, if ever, did you have to escalate, and how did you decide that was necessary?

questions.question: Describe a time you changed a senior leader's mind on something they were already committed to, without having any positional power over them.
variants: Tell me about persuading someone more senior than you to reverse a decision
questions.probes: Whether you can build a case compelling enough to overcome someone's sunk-cost attachment to their own prior decision.
pitfalls: Overstating how quickly or easily the leader changed their mind
No mention of the specific evidence or framing that actually moved them
followUps: What was the one piece of evidence or framing that actually shifted their view?
How did you approach it so it didn't feel like a challenge to their authority?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had a real conflict with an engineer or designer over the right approach, and how you resolved it.
variants: Describe disagreeing with engineering or design on direction — how did it play out?
questions.probes: Whether you can disagree on substance without pulling rank, and whether you actually incorporated their perspective or just wore them down.
pitfalls: Framing the resolution as 'I was right and eventually they agreed' with no genuine incorporation of their view
Escalating a technical or design disagreement to a manager as the first move instead of working it out directly
followUps: What part of their position turned out to be right?
How did the relationship hold up afterward?

questions.question: Describe the most significant disagreement you've had with a peer PM or a cross-functional partner.
variants: Tell me about a time you and a peer strongly disagreed on something important
questions.probes: Whether you can stay curious rather than defensive under real disagreement, and reach a resolution that isn't just capitulation from one side.
pitfalls: Making the peer sound unreasonable with no acknowledgment of their valid points
No clear resolution described
followUps: What did you learn about your own blind spot from that disagreement?
How do you two work together now?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager's decision and had to decide whether to push back or go along with it.
variants: Describe pushing back — or choosing not to — on a call your manager made
questions.probes: Whether you can disagree upward constructively, and know when to escalate your objection versus commit once a decision is made.
pitfalls: Framing 'disagree and commit' as simply going silent, without describing how you actually voiced the disagreement first
Undermining the decision after agreeing to commit to it
followUps: Once the decision was made, how did you show up in support of it?
What would have made you escalate further instead of committing?

questions.question: Walk me through a time a conflict on your team became personal rather than just professional, and how you defused it.
variants: Tell me about a disagreement that started to affect a working relationship, not just the decision at hand
questions.probes: Emotional intelligence — whether you can separate the person from the position and repair the relationship, not just resolve the immediate issue.
pitfalls: Only addressing the surface-level disagreement while ignoring the relational damage underneath
No mention of a direct, private conversation to repair the relationship
followUps: What did you say to them directly that helped defuse it?
How is that relationship now?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver a decision that you knew a stakeholder would strongly disagree with.
variants: Describe delivering unwelcome news to someone who was going to push back hard
questions.probes: How you prepared for and handled the pushback in the moment — whether you had a real rationale ready or just hoped it would go smoothly.
pitfalls: Softening the message so much the actual decision got lost
No mention of how you handled their reaction in real time
followUps: How did they react in the room, and how did you respond to that reaction?
Did you give them any way to shape the decision, or was it fully final?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to say no to someone senior who was pushing hard for a feature.
variants: Describe declining a request from leadership that you didn't think was the right call
questions.probes: Whether you can hold a position under seniority pressure using evidence and framing, rather than folding or being needlessly combative.
pitfalls: Caving after one round of pushback and building it anyway
No specific reasoning given for the no — just 'it wasn't the priority'
followUps: What evidence or framing finally got them to accept the no?
Did you offer any alternative to address their underlying concern?

questions.question: Describe a time you killed a feature that was already partially built.
variants: Tell me about cutting something that had real engineering investment already sunk into it
questions.probes: Whether you can act on sunk-cost logic correctly — recognizing that past investment shouldn't drive a future decision — and how you communicated that to the team who built it.
pitfalls: Letting sunk cost keep the feature alive past the point the data justified it
Framing it purely as a data decision with no acknowledgment of the team morale impact
followUps: How did the team that built it react, and how did you handle that?
What would you have needed to see to keep it alive instead?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to turn down a customer's specific feature request, even though saying yes would have been the easier answer.
variants: Describe declining a customer ask that would have been simple to just agree to
questions.probes: Whether you protect product coherence and long-term direction over a short-term easy yes, and how you handle the customer relationship in the no.
pitfalls: Saying yes just to avoid the difficult conversation, then having it come back to bite the roadmap later
No explanation offered to the customer for the no
followUps: How did the customer react, and did you offer them anything in place of what they asked for?
Would you make the same call again?

questions.question: Tell me about a project or product you personally decided to kill.
variants: Describe pulling the plug on something you were responsible for
questions.probes: Whether you can recognize a losing bet objectively and act on it decisively, rather than letting it limp along out of attachment or fear of admitting failure.
pitfalls: Waiting far too long past the point the data was clear, out of attachment to the work
Framing the kill decision as someone else's call to avoid owning it
followUps: What was the specific signal that finally convinced you?
What did you do with the team and resources once it was killed?

questions.question: Describe a time you recommended killing a project that wasn't yours, and had to convince the owner.
variants: Tell me about telling another PM their project should be shut down
questions.probes: Whether you can deliver a hard, evidence-based message to a peer without it becoming personal or political.
pitfalls: Going over the owner's head instead of talking to them directly first
No mention of how you framed it to make it about the evidence, not their competence
followUps: How did the project owner react, and how did that affect your relationship?
Were you right, in hindsight?

questions.question: Tell me about your biggest failure as a PM.
variants: What's a time you really got it wrong professionally?
questions.probes: Self-awareness and ownership — whether you can name a real, consequential mistake and what you actually changed because of it, not a humble-brag disguised as a failure.
pitfalls: Picking a 'failure' that's actually a thinly veiled strength ('I worked too hard')
No concrete change in behavior described afterward
followUps: What would you do differently if you were in that exact situation again today?
Who else was affected by that failure, and how did you make it right with them?

questions.question: Describe a launch you shipped that failed to move the metrics you expected, or failed outright.
variants: Tell me about a launch that just didn't work
questions.probes: Whether you can diagnose why it failed — a bad hypothesis, poor execution, wrong timing — rather than attributing it vaguely to 'the market.'
pitfalls: Blaming external factors (market conditions, timing) without examining your own hypothesis or execution
No specifics on what metric moved, or didn't, and by how much
followUps: Looking back, was the failure in the idea, the execution, or the timing?
What did you do with the feature after it failed to land?

questions.question: If you could go back, what's the one thing you'd improve about your product?
variants: Looking back at a product you've owned, what's the single change you wish you'd made?
What's one regret you have about a product you shipped?
questions.probes: Whether you have genuine, specific hindsight about your own product rather than a generic answer — this tests reflective depth, not diplomacy.
pitfalls: Giving a safe, inconsequential answer to avoid sounding critical of your own work
Picking something entirely outside your control so it doesn't reflect on your judgment
followUps: Why didn't you make that change at the time?
What would it take to make that change now?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you shipped something and only later realized it created a real problem for users.
variants: Describe a time your own launch caused unintended harm or friction for users
questions.probes: Whether you can recognize and own downstream consequences you didn't foresee, and how quickly you acted once you saw them.
pitfalls: Discovering the problem but downplaying its severity in the retelling
No mention of the actual fix or mitigation, only the discovery
followUps: How did you find out it was a problem — did users tell you, or did you catch it in the data?
How long did it take to fix once you knew?

questions.question: Describe a time you gave leadership a forecast or projection that turned out to be significantly wrong.
variants: Tell me about a time your numbers were off, and how that landed with leadership
questions.probes: Whether you own the miss transparently and can explain what was wrong with your model or assumptions, rather than minimizing the gap.
pitfalls: Minimizing how far off the forecast actually was
No explanation of what assumption in the model was flawed
followUps: What assumption turned out to be the flawed one?
How did you rebuild credibility with leadership after that?

questions.question: Tell me about a complex problem you solved.
variants: Walk me through the most complicated problem you've had to untangle
Describe a genuinely hard, multi-layered problem you worked through
questions.probes: Whether you can break a messy, multi-dimensional problem into tractable pieces and actually reach a resolution, not just describe how hard it was.
pitfalls: Spending the whole answer establishing how complex the problem was, with too little time left for the actual resolution
No clear articulation of what made it complex — multiple stakeholders, unclear data, technical constraints — versus just 'a lot of work'
followUps: What made this more complex than a typical problem you'd face?
What was the turning point where it started to become tractable?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to make a significant product decision with no data available at all to guide you.
variants: Tell me about deciding something important with zero data to lean on
questions.probes: Whether you can reason from first principles, analogous situations, and qualitative signal, and still commit — rather than freezing or defaulting to whoever's opinion is loudest.
pitfalls: Waiting for data that was never going to arrive in time, stalling the decision
Presenting the eventual decision as obvious in hindsight, hiding how uncertain it actually felt at the time
followUps: What reasoning did you use in place of data?
How did you know when you had enough conviction to act?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to prioritize under real time pressure, with more urgent asks than your team could handle.
variants: Describe a moment everything felt like the top priority and you had to pick
questions.probes: Whether you have and can articulate an actual framework for trade-offs under pressure, rather than defaulting to whoever escalated loudest.
pitfalls: Prioritizing based on who complained the most rather than actual impact
No framework or criteria mentioned — just 'I made a judgment call'
followUps: What criteria did you use to rank the competing asks?
What did you deliberately choose not to do, and how did that land with the people who wanted it?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to reprioritize an entire roadmap mid-quarter because of a new piece of information.
variants: Tell me about a significant roadmap change you had to make partway through
questions.probes: Whether you can recognize when new information genuinely warrants disruption versus chasing every shiny new signal.
pitfalls: Changing the roadmap too easily, signaling a lack of conviction in the original plan
No mention of how you communicated the change to the team already executing against the old plan
followUps: How did the team react to the roadmap change mid-flight?
In hindsight, was the reprioritization worth the disruption it caused?

questions.question: Tell me about a time two equally important initiatives were competing for the same limited engineering resources, and you had to choose.
variants: Describe choosing between two genuinely important projects with only enough capacity for one
questions.probes: Whether you can make and defend a genuinely hard trade-off rather than finding a way to claim you did both.
pitfalls: Claiming you found a way to 'do both' when really one got shortchanged without saying so
No mention of how you handled the disappointment of whoever owned the deprioritized initiative
followUps: What tipped the decision in favor of the one you picked?
What happened to the initiative you didn't pick?

questions.question: Walk me through how you prioritized features for a 0-to-1 product with far more good ideas than you had time to build.
variants: Tell me about narrowing a big backlog down to an actual V1
questions.probes: Whether you can ruthlessly scope to what proves the core hypothesis, rather than trying to include everything that sounds valuable.
pitfalls: Including too much in V1 because everything genuinely sounded valuable
No clear criteria for what made the cut versus what didn't
followUps: What was the one feature you almost cut but kept, and why?
What did you add in V2 that you'd originally deprioritized?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to prioritize a small but urgent bug fix over a big strategic initiative you were excited about.
variants: Describe dropping strategic work for something more urgent but less exciting
questions.probes: Whether you can set aside your own excitement or ego in favor of what the business actually needs in the moment.
pitfalls: Resenting the interruption visibly instead of handling it professionally
Downplaying how much the urgent fix actually mattered, to make the story feel more strategic
followUps: How did you get back to the strategic work afterward?
How did you decide it was actually urgent enough to warrant the switch?

questions.question: Tell me about a time direct contact with a customer changed a decision you were about to make.
variants: Describe a moment talking to a real user completely shifted your thinking
questions.probes: Whether you actively seek out unfiltered customer contact, and whether it genuinely changes your decisions or just confirms what you already believed.
pitfalls: The customer interaction conveniently confirms exactly what you already wanted to do
No specific quote, moment, or detail from the actual conversation
followUps: What exactly did the customer say that changed your mind?
How often do you talk to customers directly versus relying on secondhand research?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to design for a user whose context was very different from your own.
variants: Tell me about building for a user very unlike yourself
questions.probes: Whether you can genuinely step outside your own assumptions and context rather than projecting your own habits onto a different user base.
pitfalls: Assuming your own usage patterns and preferences generalize to a very different user
No specific method described for how you actually understood their context (field visits, interviews, data)
followUps: What was the biggest wrong assumption you started with?
How did you validate you'd actually understood their context correctly?

questions.question: Tell me about a time user research surfaced something that contradicted your own hypothesis.
variants: Describe a moment research proved you wrong about what users wanted
questions.probes: Whether you run research to genuinely learn versus to validate a decision you'd already made, and whether you actually acted on the contradiction.
pitfalls: Research 'discovering' exactly what you expected it to, with no genuine surprise
Acknowledging the contradictory finding but not actually changing course because of it
followUps: What did you do differently because of that finding?
How did you make sure the research questions weren't leading users toward your hypothesis?

questions.question: Describe a time you ran user research with a very small or imperfect sample and had to decide how much to trust it.
variants: Tell me about drawing conclusions from research you knew wasn't statistically ideal
questions.probes: Whether you understand the limits of qualitative and small-sample research and calibrate your confidence accordingly.
pitfalls: Treating five user interviews as if they carried the statistical weight of a large quantitative study
No mention of triangulating the finding with any other source of evidence
followUps: How did you triangulate that finding with other evidence before acting on it?
What would have made you distrust the finding instead?

questions.question: Tell me about a metric you were accountable for and how you moved it.
variants: Walk me through owning a number and actually improving it
questions.probes: Whether you can trace a clear causal chain from the actions you took to the metric moving, rather than claiming credit for a number that moved for other reasons.
pitfalls: Taking credit for a metric improvement that was likely driven by something outside your control (seasonality, another team's launch)
No specific magnitude or timeframe given for the improvement
followUps: How do you know your specific changes caused the movement, versus something else?
What guardrail metric did you watch to make sure you weren't gaming it?

questions.question: Describe a time a metric you owned moved in the wrong direction despite your team's best efforts, and how you handled reporting that upward.
variants: Tell me about a number that got worse on your watch
questions.probes: Whether you report bad news transparently and quickly rather than delaying or dressing it up, and whether you can diagnose the real cause.
pitfalls: Delaying reporting the bad number, hoping it would self-correct before anyone noticed
Blaming external factors without a genuine root-cause investigation
followUps: How quickly did you flag it once you noticed?
What was the actual root cause, once you dug in?

questions.question: Tell me about an A/B test whose result surprised you.
variants: Describe an experiment that didn't go the way you expected
questions.probes: Whether you can honestly interpret a result that contradicts your hypothesis, rather than explaining it away or rerunning until you get the answer you wanted.
pitfalls: Rerunning or re-slicing the experiment repeatedly until it shows the desired result
Dismissing a valid but unwelcome result as 'noise' without statistical justification
followUps: What did you do differently as a result of that surprising finding?
How did you rule out that it was just statistical noise?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to decide whether an experiment's result was strong enough to ship, when the data was borderline.
variants: Tell me about a close call on whether to ship a test result
questions.probes: Whether you understand statistical significance, practical significance, and business risk well enough to make a defensible borderline call.
pitfalls: Shipping a marginal result purely because you wanted a positive story to tell
No mention of the actual confidence level or effect size involved
followUps: What was the actual effect size and confidence level?
What would you have needed to see to not ship it?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you deliberately phased or staged a launch to de-risk it.
variants: Describe rolling something out gradually instead of all at once
questions.probes: Whether you can design a rollout plan with real go/no-go criteria at each stage, rather than a phased launch that's phased in name only.
pitfalls: No concrete criteria described for what would have stopped or reversed the rollout at each stage
Describing the phasing as a formality rather than something that actually informed decisions along the way
followUps: What would have made you pull back at an earlier stage?
Did anything from an early phase actually change your plan for the next one?

questions.question: Describe a phased rollout that stalled in beta far longer than intended, and how you got it unstuck.
variants: Tell me about a launch that got stuck in an extended pilot phase
questions.probes: Whether you can diagnose why a beta stalled — usually unclear success criteria or organizational fear — and force a real decision.
pitfalls: Letting the beta run indefinitely without ever forcing a go/no-go decision
No mention of what specifically was blocking the full rollout
followUps: What was actually blocking it from graduating out of beta?
What finally forced the decision to move forward or kill it?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to slow down or change a launch because of a legal, regulatory, or compliance concern.
variants: Describe a launch that got delayed or reshaped by a compliance issue
questions.probes: Whether you take regulatory and legal risk seriously as a genuine product constraint, rather than treating compliance as a rubber stamp to route around.
pitfalls: Treating legal/compliance as an obstacle to work around instead of a legitimate constraint to design within
No specifics on what the actual regulatory concern was
followUps: How did you redesign the feature to satisfy the concern without gutting the value?
How early did you loop in legal or compliance, in hindsight — early enough?

questions.question: Describe a time you identified a privacy or data-risk issue in a product before it became a real problem.
variants: Tell me about catching a data or privacy risk proactively
questions.probes: Whether you proactively think about data risk as part of product design, rather than only reacting after a breach or complaint.
pitfalls: The 'catch' actually happening after a near-miss or complaint, not proactively as claimed
No specifics about what data was at risk or how
followUps: What made you think to check for that risk in the first place?
What process did you put in place afterward to catch similar issues earlier?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to go deep on a technical trade-off to make the right product call.
variants: Describe a moment you had to really understand the engineering constraints before deciding
questions.probes: Whether you can engage substantively with technical trade-offs (latency, scalability, tech debt) rather than deferring the decision entirely to engineering.
pitfalls: Deferring the entire decision to engineering with no independent product judgment applied
Overstating your own technical fluency in a way that wouldn't survive a follow-up question
followUps: What was the specific trade-off, in technical terms?
How did you validate your understanding of the constraint with the engineering team?

questions.question: Describe a time you pushed back on an engineering estimate because you believed there was a simpler technical path.
variants: Tell me about questioning an engineering timeline or approach
questions.probes: Whether you can engage credibly on technical scope without overstepping into engineering's actual expertise.
pitfalls: Pushing back on the estimate with no real technical basis, purely because you wanted it faster
Damaging trust with engineering by being right in a way that felt like a gotcha
followUps: Were you right about the simpler path, in the end?
How did you raise it in a way that didn't feel like second-guessing their expertise?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you mentored someone — a junior PM, an intern, or someone outside your direct team.
variants: Describe helping someone grow professionally, even without a formal reporting relationship
questions.probes: Whether you invest genuinely in others' growth, and can point to a specific, measurable change in them, not just time spent together.
pitfalls: Describing time spent together with no specific growth or outcome for the person mentored
Taking too much credit for their growth rather than crediting their own effort
followUps: What's the most specific piece of feedback or advice you gave them?
Where are they now, and how did that mentoring affect their trajectory?

questions.question: Describe a time a mentee or junior teammate pushed back on your advice, and how you handled it.
variants: Tell me about someone you were mentoring disagreeing with your guidance
questions.probes: Whether you can hold a mentoring relationship with genuine two-way respect, rather than expecting your advice to be taken uncritically.
pitfalls: Dismissing their pushback simply because of the seniority gap
No acknowledgment of whether their pushback turned out to have a point
followUps: Did their pushback turn out to be right, in hindsight?
How did that change how you mentor since then?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to give someone difficult feedback they didn't want to hear.
variants: Describe delivering hard feedback to a peer or teammate
questions.probes: Whether you can be direct and specific without being harsh, and whether the feedback actually landed and changed behavior.
pitfalls: Softening the feedback so much the actual message got lost
No mention of whether the person's behavior actually changed afterward
followUps: How did they react in the moment, and how did that change over time?
What would you do differently in how you delivered it?

questions.question: Describe the toughest piece of feedback you've ever received, and what you did with it.
variants: Tell me about a time someone gave you hard feedback about yourself
questions.probes: Whether you can take criticism without getting defensive, and show a real, specific behavior change as a result — not just polite acceptance.
pitfalls: Claiming to have 'taken it well' with no specific evidence of what actually changed afterward
Picking feedback that's actually flattering in disguise
followUps: What specifically did you change in how you work because of that feedback?
How did you feel in the moment you received it, honestly?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you faced an ethical call where the most profitable option and the right option for the user weren't the same thing.
variants: Describe a moment doing right by the user cost the business something
questions.probes: Whether you have a genuine ethical compass that shows up in a real trade-off, not just a stated value that's never actually been tested.
pitfalls: Presenting a decision as an ethical dilemma when it was actually a clear-cut, low-stakes call
The 'right' choice conveniently costing the business nothing at all
followUps: What did it actually cost the business to make the ethical choice?
Did leadership support that call, or did you have to push for it?

questions.question: Describe a time you noticed a product pattern (dark pattern, misleading copy, aggressive nudge) that worked but felt wrong, and what you did about it.
variants: Tell me about pushing back on a growth tactic that crossed a line for you
questions.probes: Whether you can distinguish persuasive design from manipulation and act on that distinction even when the manipulative version performs better.
pitfalls: Not being specific about what made the pattern actually manipulative rather than just aggressive
No mention of the performance cost of removing or softening it
followUps: What was the actual performance impact of changing it?
Where do you personally draw the line between persuasive and manipulative design?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to rally a discouraged or burnt-out team to keep pushing on a hard project.
variants: Describe leading a team through a low point on a project
questions.probes: Whether you can read and address team morale directly, not just push harder on the roadmap and hope motivation follows.
pitfalls: Only addressing the roadmap or timeline, with no attention to actual team morale
Taking sole credit for the team's recovery rather than crediting the team
followUps: What specifically did you do to address morale, versus just the work itself?
How did you know the team had actually recovered, not just gone quiet?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to make an unpopular call as the leader of a cross-functional initiative.
variants: Tell me about a decision that wasn't well received by the team you were leading
questions.probes: Whether you can absorb the unpopularity of a necessary decision without either backing down or becoming defensive about it.
pitfalls: Softening the description of how unpopular it actually was
No mention of how you addressed the team's concerns directly, even while holding the decision
followUps: How did you communicate the decision to the team who disagreed with it?
Would you make the same call again?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to cut scope significantly to hit a hard deadline.
variants: Describe shrinking a project's scope under real time pressure
questions.probes: Whether you can distinguish what's essential from what's nice-to-have under real pressure, and communicate the cut transparently rather than quietly dropping it.
pitfalls: Cutting corners on quality instead of scope, and not admitting that's what happened
Not clearly communicating to stakeholders what was cut and why
followUps: What was the first thing you cut, and how did you decide?
What was the cost of cutting that scope — did it show up later?

questions.question: Describe a time you had to deliver a project after losing a key team member partway through.
variants: Tell me about executing through unexpected loss of resources mid-project
questions.probes: Whether you can replan and reprioritize under a real, unplanned resource hit rather than just working harder to absorb the gap.
pitfalls: Framing it purely as personal heroics rather than a genuine replanning of scope or timeline
No mention of how the remaining team's workload or morale was managed
followUps: What did you cut or delay because of the resourcing hit?
How did the rest of the team absorb the extra load?

questions.question: Why product management, and not another function?
variants: What drew you to product management specifically?
Why did you choose to become a PM?
questions.probes: Whether your motivation is specific and grounded in real experience, not a generic answer about 'liking to build things.'
pitfalls: A generic answer that could apply equally to almost any function
No specific formative moment or experience behind the choice
followUps: What's a moment that first made you think 'this is the job I want'?
What function did you consider instead, and why didn't you go that way?

questions.question: Why this company, specifically, and why now?
variants: What made you want to join us over other options you likely have?
Why here, and why this point in your career?
questions.probes: Whether you've done real homework on the company's specific product, strategy, or challenges, versus giving an answer that could be recycled for any interview.
pitfalls: An answer generic enough to be reused verbatim in any other interview
Praising the company in the abstract with no reference to a specific product, challenge, or strategic bet they're making
followUps: What's a specific product decision of ours you'd have made differently?
What's the biggest risk you see in our strategy right now?

questions.question: Walk me through your career arc and how each move led logically to this one.
variants: Tell me your story — how did you get from where you started to sitting here today?
questions.probes: Whether you can tell a coherent narrative connecting your choices, rather than a list of jobs with no throughline.
pitfalls: A disconnected list of roles with no narrative thread tying them together
Spending too long on early career details and rushing the part most relevant to this role
followUps: What's the one thread that connects all of these moves?
What would you tell yourself at the start of your career, knowing what you know now?
